hooks.text: Astronomers first saw a faint violet speck, calling it an ordinary star.
This faint blue dot is actually heavier than forty billion Suns.
A tiny photographic speck hid a shadow forty times wider than Pluto's orbit.

title: The Faint Blue Star That Held 40 Billion Suns
description: Mistaken for a faint star in 1957, TON 618 is actually an ultramassive black hole that outshines 140 trillion Suns.

beats.text: Astronomers first saw a faint violet speck, calling it an ordinary star.
beats.visual: Historical photographic survey plate showing faint stars from Tonantzintla Observatory, 1957

beats.text: In 1957, Mexican astronomers catalogued it as entry 618, unaware of the monster lurking 10.8 billion light-years away.
beats.visual: Portrait of astronomers Braulio Iriarte and Enrique Chavira, 1950s

beats.text: This point of light is an ultramassive black hole with an event horizon radius of 1,300 astronomical units.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a supermassive black hole with a glowing accretion disk, NASA, 2019

beats.text: That is 40 times Pluto’s distance from the Sun, all contained within one dark sphere.
beats.visual: Diagram comparing the event horizon of TON 618 to the orbit of Pluto, 2020
queries: Black hole size comparison solar system

beats.text: Gas whipping around the void at 10,000 kilometers per second fuels a brilliance equal to 140 trillion Suns.
beats.visual: Animation of gas spinning at relativistic speeds around a black hole, NASA, 2014

beats.text: Initial measurements found 66 billion solar masses, later revised to 40.7 billion Suns.
beats.visual: H-beta and C IV emission lines on an astronomical spectrum chart, 2018

beats.text: Wrapped in a glowing hydrogen nebula over 300,000 light-years across, it remains one of the heaviest objects in existence.
beats.visual: Artist impression of a massive Lyman-alpha nebula surrounding a quasar, ESO, 2016

beats.text: No monster in the cosmos has ever hidden behind such a quiet disguise.
beats.visual: Deep wide-field photograph of stars in the constellation Canes Venatici, 2021
